metadata.title: Consensus Isn't Verification.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why doesn't several AI models agreeing on an answer count as verification? Lands the carry-out that agreement between AI checkers built on similar training is the same blind spot, counted twice, not independent evidence.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B08 (the order-swap demo: same two answers, judge verdict flips with position, not content; returned as the reel closes)
metadata.one_flag: B07 - a check only counts as independent if it doesn't itself quietly run on the same kind of model underneath

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes three AI judges agreeing proves an answer is verified. It doesn't — agreement like that is just consensus. So the real question: when AI checks AI, is agreement ever actually verification?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Three AI judges agree. That means it's verified, right?', hesitates on 'verified', corrects to 'consensus'

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('verified' -> 'consensus') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: It's increasingly common to have one AI system check another one's work — grading an answer, reviewing code, auditing a claim. When several AI reviewers look at the same output and agree, that agreement gets treated as proof the answer is correct.

shot.new_visual_element: several AI reviewer cards converging on one output, a checkmark forming where they agree

production_viz.label: AI checking AI
production_viz.mechanic: Three small reviewer cards labeled REVIEWER arranged above one OUTPUT card. Arrows from each reviewer converge on the output. A checkmark forms at the point where all three arrows meet, labeled 'THEY AGREE'.

beats.narration_text: That seems reasonable. More opinions converging on the same verdict looks like stronger evidence — the way several judges reaching the same score, or several doctors agreeing on a diagnosis, makes you more confident, not less.

shot.new_visual_element: the reviewer cards relabeled JUDGES / DOCTORS, all pointing to one confident verdict

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: The B01 composition relabeled: the three reviewer cards become JUDGE, JUDGE, DOCTOR. A single large 'VERDICT' card glows terracotta beneath them with a confident checkmark, captioned 'more agreement = more confidence?'.

beats.narration_text: Here's a test. Give an AI judge the same two answers twice — once in order A, once with the order swapped. Nothing about the answers changed. But the judge's verdict flipped: it picked whichever answer came first, not whichever answer was better.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - two identical answer cards, order swapped between two runs, the winner flips

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - same answers, order swapped
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Two identical answer cards, A and B. RUN 1: order A-then-B, judge picks A (terracotta ring). RUN 2: order B-then-A, same two cards, judge picks B (terracotta ring shifts). Caption: 'NOTHING CHANGED BUT THE ORDER'. THIS EXACT PAIR RETURNS AT B08.

beats.narration_text: That's not a glitch — it's one of three documented judging biases: favoring the first answer shown, favoring the longer answer, and favoring answers that sound like its own style. These are structural, and they show up whenever an AI model checks another AI's output.

shot.new_visual_element: three labeled bias cards: POSITION, LENGTH, STYLE

production_viz.label: Three documented biases
production_viz.mechanic: Three pill cards in a row: POSITION BIAS ('favors first shown'), LENGTH BIAS ('favors longer'), STYLE BIAS ('favors its own style'). A caption beneath reads 'STRUCTURAL, NOT A BUG', underlined in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Cross-checking only reduces error when the checkers fail independently. If two checkers share the same blind spots, their agreement tells you nothing new. AI models built on similar training data and similar tuning share exactly that — the same blind spots. Agreement between them is evidence they share priors, not evidence they're both right.

shot.new_visual_element: two overlapping circles, the shared region marked; agreement lives only inside the overlap

production_viz.label: Where agreement actually lives
production_viz.mechanic: Two circles labeled MODEL A and MODEL B overlap. The overlap region fills terracotta, captioned 'SHARED TRAINING, SHARED BLIND SPOTS'. A small arrow points into the overlap labeled 'their agreement lives here'.

beats.narration_text: The fix isn't zero AI — it's pairing each kind of claim with a check that fails differently. A factual claim gets checked against a retrieval lookup. A math result gets checked by running the actual code. A schema or format claim gets checked by a validator. None of those share the model's blind spots.

shot.new_visual_element: a small pairing table: claim type -> independent check, each row landing outside the shared-bias circle

production_viz.label: Pair with a different failure mode
production_viz.mechanic: A three-row table: FACTUAL CLAIM -> RETRIEVAL LOOKUP; MATH RESULT -> RUN THE CODE; SCHEMA / FORMAT -> VALIDATOR. Each right-hand box sits outside a faint dashed circle labeled 'MODEL BLIND SPOTS', with a small arrow showing it lands clear of the circle.

beats.narration_text: One flag — a check only counts as independent if it doesn't quietly run on the same kind of model underneath. A search index built by an AI, or a validator whose rules an AI wrote, can reintroduce the exact blind spot it was supposed to catch.

shot.new_visual_element: THE FLAG - a clean check card, a hidden AI gear revealed inside it

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG - is the check really independent?
production_viz.mechanic: A single terracotta FLAG marker over the beat, the reel's only hedge, labeled as one. A 'VALIDATOR' card looks clean on the outside; it cracks open to reveal a small gear icon labeled 'built by an AI' hidden inside — the blind spot smuggled back in.

beats.narration_text: So this cuts both ways. When a code check and an AI's claim agree, that's real evidence — their failure modes don't overlap. When three AI judges agree, that alone still proves nothing — swap the order, and the "verified" answer flips. And when AI judges disagree, that doesn't prove one is wrong either — it can just mean the same shared bias landed differently this run.

shot.new_visual_element: mirrored panel: INDEPENDENT AGREE (holds) vs. THE ANCHOR RETURNS, order swapped, verdict flips

production_viz.label: Both directions, then the anchor closes
production_viz.mechanic: Left: CODE CHECK and AI CLAIM cards agreeing, a solid checkmark, captioned 'REAL EVIDENCE'. Right: THE B03 ANCHOR RETURNS, identical two-card order-swap, verdict flipping again, captioned 'STILL PROVES NOTHING'. Bottom: two dimmed disagreeing judge cards, captioned 'DISAGREEMENT DOESN'T PROVE EITHER WRONG'.

beats.narration_text: More AI models agreeing isn't more verification. It's the same blind spot, counted twice.

props.quote: More AI models agreeing isn't more verification. It's the same blind spot, counted twice.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I want to find correlated-failure seams in an AI pipeline I use. Look at how outputs get checked, and tell me every place where an AI call is verifying another AI's output. For each one, tell me if the checker could share the same blind spot as what it's checking, and suggest a structurally different way to verify it instead — a retrieval lookup, running actual code, a schema validator, or a named human reviewer. Liam, in for Bear.
